questions.q: Science is the study of
questions.explain: Science is the study of natural phenomena, the things that happen in the natural world. It is done both inside and outside the laboratory.
questions.lo: State that science is the study of natural phenomena, in and out of the laboratory

notes.0: Science is not limited to the laboratory. Scientists also study things outdoors, such as weather, rocks and animals in their habitats.
notes.1: Science covers non-living things too, such as light, rocks, weather and stars, not only plants and animals.
notes.2: Science deals with what can be observed and tested. Opinions cannot be tested, so they are not what science studies.

questions.q: Quantitative data is collected using
questions.explain: Quantitative data are numbers with units. These numbers come from measuring with instruments such as rulers, balances and thermometers.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.1: Descriptions in words are qualitative data. Quantitative data are numbers, so think about what gives a number reading.
notes.2: Smell gives a description, not a number. Quantitative data need a reading that is a number with a unit.
notes.3: A drawing records what something looks like. It does not give a number, so it is qualitative data.

questions.q: Qualitative data is usually expressed as
questions.explain: Qualitative data describe qualities such as colour, texture or smell. They are recorded in words or drawings, not as numbers.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.0: Numbers with units are quantitative data. Qualitative data describe qualities such as colour or texture.
notes.1: A reading on a scale is a measurement, so it gives quantitative data. Qualitative data describe qualities without measuring.
notes.3: SI units are used for measured quantities, which are quantitative data. Qualitative data do not have units.

questions.q: "The coconut shell is hard and smooth." What type of data is this?
questions.explain: Hard and smooth are descriptions of the shell in words. No measurement or number is given, so the data is qualitative.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.0: Quantitative data must contain a measured number with a unit. Check whether the sentence has any number at all.
notes.2: For both types, the sentence needs a description and a measured number. This sentence has no number in it.

why.right: The shell data is qualitative because it describes the shell in words without any measured number.
wrong: The shell data is qualitative because it was collected by touching the shell instead of looking at it.
The shell data is qualitative because it is about an object that is found in nature.

questions.q: "The coconut has a mass of 1.2 kg." What type of data is this?
questions.explain: A mass of 1.2 kg is a number with a unit, measured with a balance. Measured numbers are quantitative data.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.0: Qualitative data describe qualities in words. This sentence gives a measured number with a unit.
notes.2: To be both types, the sentence also needs a description in words, such as colour or texture. It only gives a measurement.

why.right: The coconut data is quantitative because it is a measured number with a unit.
wrong: The coconut data is quantitative because mass is a property that every object has.
The coconut data is quantitative because it was written down as a full sentence.

questions.q: "The chair is taller than the table." What type of data is this?
questions.explain: The sentence compares the chair and the table in words. No measured number with a unit is given, so the data is qualitative.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.1: For both types, a measured number with a unit is needed as well as a description. This sentence has no number.
notes.2: Taller is a comparison, not a measurement. Quantitative data need a measured number with a unit, and none is given here.

why.right: The chair data is qualitative because it compares heights in words without giving a measured number.
wrong: The chair data is qualitative because height can never be measured with an instrument.
The chair data is qualitative because it compares two objects instead of describing one.

questions.q: "The orange juice tasted sour and was at 8 °C." What type of data is this?
questions.explain: Sour is a description in words, which is qualitative. 8 °C is a measured number with a unit, which is quantitative. The sentence contains both.
questions.lo: Classify data as qualitative or quantitative

notes.0: 8 °C is quantitative, but the sentence also describes the taste as sour. Check every part of the sentence.
notes.1: Sour is qualitative, but the sentence also gives a temperature reading. Check every part of the sentence.

why.right: The juice data is both types because it has a description in words and a measured number with a unit.
wrong: The juice data is both types because it was collected using two different senses.
The juice data is both types because it describes two different properties of the same drink.

questions.q: Scientific knowledge must be based on
questions.explain: Scientific knowledge must be supported by evidence from observations and experiments. This evidence can be checked and tested by others.
questions.lo: Describe the nature of scientific knowledge (evidence-based, open to change, multiple interpretations)

notes.0: Science does not decide by vote. Many people can believe something that is not supported by observations or experiments.
notes.1: Feelings differ from person to person and cannot be tested. Science needs something that others can check.
notes.2: Imagination helps scientists think of ideas, but an idea is only accepted once it is supported by what is observed or measured.

why.right: Scientific knowledge rests on evidence because observations and measurements can be checked and repeated by others.
wrong: Scientific knowledge rests on evidence because evidence never changes once it has been collected.
Scientific knowledge rests on evidence because evidence is always agreed on by everyone who sees it.

questions.q: When can scientific knowledge be changed?
choices: when most people disagree with it
when a famous scientist says so
when the scientific community accepts new evidence
questions.explain: Scientific knowledge changes when new evidence is found and the scientific community checks and accepts it.
questions.lo: Describe the nature of scientific knowledge (evidence-based, open to change, multiple interpretations)

notes.0: Scientific ideas are not changed by popular opinion. A change needs something that can be observed or measured and then checked.
notes.1: Old ideas stay in use as long as the evidence supports them. Age alone is not a reason to change scientific knowledge.
notes.2: Even a famous scientist must support a claim with evidence that other scientists can check. Fame alone does not change knowledge.

why.right: Scientific knowledge changes after new evidence is checked by many scientists and found to be reliable.
wrong: Scientific knowledge changes after a set number of years because ideas need to be updated regularly.
Scientific knowledge changes after the most senior scientist decides that an idea is out of date.

questions.q: Two scientists study the same data but reach different conclusions. This shows that
choices: one of the scientists must be dishonest
evidence can be interpreted in different ways
questions.explain: Scientists can look at the same evidence and interpret it differently. Different conclusions do not mean the data or the scientists are wrong.
questions.lo: Describe the nature of scientific knowledge (evidence-based, open to change, multiple interpretations)

notes.0: Correct data can still lead to different conclusions. The difference comes from how the data is explained, not from the data itself.
notes.1: Different conclusions are a normal part of science. Honest scientists can explain the same data in different ways.
notes.3: Both scientists are studying data, so they are using evidence. The question is about how that evidence is explained.

why.right: Different conclusions can come from the same data because scientists may explain the evidence in different ways.
wrong: Different conclusions can come from the same data because data changes each time someone looks at it.
Different conclusions can come from the same data because one scientist always makes a mistake.

questions.q: A proposed explanation for an observation that can be tested is a
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation for an observation. It can be tested by doing an experiment.
questions.lo: Identify a hypothesis and a scientific question

notes.1: A conclusion is stated after the experiment, based on the results. The term needed is the explanation proposed before testing.
notes.2: A variable is a factor that can change in an experiment. It is not an explanation of an observation.
notes.3: A result is what is observed or measured during an experiment. The term needed is the explanation suggested before the test.

questions.q: Which is a scientific question?
choices: How does temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?
Why are cookies eaten at festivals?
questions.explain: A scientific question can be answered by testing and measuring. The effect of temperature on how fast sugar dissolves can be measured in an experiment.
questions.lo: Identify a hypothesis and a scientific question

notes.0: The best flavour is a matter of personal opinion. A scientific question must be answerable by measuring or observing.
notes.2: Which cookie looks nicest depends on personal taste. It cannot be answered by a fair test with measurements.
notes.3: This is about culture and tradition. It cannot be tested with an experiment that measures variables.

why.right: A scientific question can be tested, since its answer comes from measuring a variable in an experiment.
wrong: A scientific question can be tested, since it starts with the word how instead of why.
A scientific question can be tested, since most people would give the same answer to it.

questions.q: In a fair experiment, how many variables are changed?
questions.explain: In a fair test, only one variable is changed. All other variables are kept constant, so any effect can be linked to that one change.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.0: If several variables change, the cause of any difference in results cannot be identified. A fair test changes as few as possible.
notes.1: With two variables changed, it is unclear which one caused the result. A fair test keeps every other variable constant.
notes.2: Changing every variable makes it impossible to tell what caused the result. A fair test keeps most variables constant.

why.right: A fair test changes one variable so that any change in the results can be linked to that variable.
wrong: A fair test changes one variable so that the experiment takes less time and uses less equipment.
A fair test changes one variable so that the results always match the hypothesis.

questions.q: A student tests how sugar mass affects jelly setting time. Which is the variable changed?
questions.explain: The variable changed is the one the student changes on purpose. Here the student changes the sugar mass to see its effect on setting time.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.0: The fridge temperature could affect setting time, so it should be kept constant. It is not what the student is testing.
notes.2: Setting time is the result that the student records. Look for the variable the student changes on purpose.
notes.3: The volume of water should stay the same so the test is fair. It is not the factor being tested.

why.right: Sugar mass is the variable changed because the student chooses different values of it on purpose.
wrong: Sugar mass is the variable changed because it is the variable that takes longest to measure.
Sugar mass is the variable changed because it is the result recorded at the end.

questions.q: A student tests how sugar mass affects jelly setting time. Which is the variable measured?
questions.explain: The variable measured is the result recorded in the experiment. The student measures how long the jelly takes to set for each sugar mass.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.1: The volume of water should be kept constant for a fair test. It is not the result being recorded.
notes.2: The fridge temperature should be kept constant. It is a condition of the test, not the result being recorded.
notes.3: Sugar mass is chosen by the student on purpose. The variable measured is the result that depends on it.

why.right: Jelly setting time is the variable measured because it is the result that depends on the sugar mass.
wrong: Jelly setting time is the variable measured because the student chooses its value before starting.
Jelly setting time is the variable measured because it stays the same in every trial.

questions.q: A student tests how ramp height affects a toy car's speed. Which is kept constant?
questions.explain: The mass of the toy car could affect the results, so it must be kept the same. Then only the ramp height is changed.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.0: Speed is the result that the student measures. It is expected to change, so it cannot be kept constant.
notes.1: Ramp height is what the student changes on purpose. It is not kept constant.

why.right: Keeping the car's mass constant makes the test fair, since only the ramp height is then being changed.
wrong: Keeping the car's mass constant makes the test fair, since a heavier car cannot roll down a ramp.
Keeping the car's mass constant makes the test fair, since it keeps the speed the same in every trial.

questions.q: A student tests how ramp height affects a toy car's speed. Which is the variable measured?
questions.explain: The variable measured is the result recorded. The student records the speed of the toy car for each ramp height.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.1: The ramp length should be kept constant for a fair test. It is not the result being recorded.
notes.2: Ramp height is changed on purpose by the student. The variable measured is the result that depends on it.
notes.3: The car's mass should be kept the same in every trial. It is not the result being recorded.

why.right: The car's speed is the variable measured because it is the result that depends on the ramp height.
wrong: The car's speed is the variable measured because the student sets it before each trial.
The car's speed is the variable measured because it is kept the same in every trial.

questions.q: Only the amount of light given to identical plants is changed. What is being investigated?
questions.explain: Only the amount of light is changed, and the plants are identical. So the investigation tests how light affects plant growth.
questions.lo: Identify the variable changed, measured and kept constant

notes.0: The plants are identical, so plant type is kept the same. The investigation is about the one factor that changes.
notes.1: Water is not mentioned as changing, so it should be kept constant. Look at which factor is changed.
notes.3: Soil is not the factor being changed. The investigation tests the effect of the one variable that changes.

why.right: The plant investigation tests light because the variable changed is the factor whose effect is being studied.
wrong: The plant investigation tests light because plants need light more than they need water or soil.
The plant investigation tests light because light is the easiest variable to keep constant.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of mass?
questions.explain: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: N is the newton, the unit of force. Mass and force are different quantities.
notes.2: The gram is a unit of mass, but it is not the SI unit. The SI unit of mass is 1000 times larger.
notes.3: The milligram is a unit of mass, but it is far smaller than the SI unit of mass.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of length?
questions.explain: The SI unit of length is the metre (m). Other units such as cm, mm and km are based on it.
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: The centimetre is a unit of length, but it is one hundredth of the SI unit of length.
notes.1: The millimetre is a unit of length, but it is one thousandth of the SI unit of length.
notes.2: The kilometre is a unit of length, but it is 1000 times the SI unit of length.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of time?
questions.explain: The SI unit of time is the second (s).
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.1: The hour is a common unit of time, but it is not the SI unit. One hour is 3600 of the SI unit.
notes.2: The minute is a common unit of time, but it is not the SI unit. One minute is 60 of the SI unit.
notes.3: The millisecond is one thousandth of the SI unit of time. It is not the SI unit itself.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of temperature?
questions.explain: The SI unit of temperature is the kelvin (K). Degrees Celsius is used in daily life but is not the SI unit.
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: J is the joule, the unit of energy. Temperature is a different quantity from energy.
notes.1: Degrees Celsius is used in daily life and in the laboratory, but it is not the SI unit of temperature.
notes.2: Degrees Fahrenheit is used in some countries, but it is not the SI unit of temperature.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of volume?
questions.explain: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre (m³). Units such as ml, cm³ and l are smaller units often used for liquids.
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: The millilitre is commonly used for liquids, but it is not the SI unit of volume.
notes.1: The cubic centimetre is a unit of volume, but it is based on the centimetre, which is not the SI unit of length.
notes.3: The litre is a common unit for liquids, but it is not the SI unit of volume.

questions.q: Which SI unit is not correct?
questions.explain: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram, not the gram. The other three pairs are correct SI units.
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: This pair is correct, since the second is the SI unit of time. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.2: This pair is correct, since the kelvin is the SI unit of temperature. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.3: This pair is correct, since the metre is the SI unit of length. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.

questions.q: Which quantity has the SI unit kelvin (K)?
questions.explain: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature.
questions.lo: State the SI units of mass, length, time, temperature and volume

notes.0: The SI unit of length is the metre. The kelvin measures a different quantity.
notes.2: The SI unit of mass is the kilogram. The kelvin measures a different quantity.
notes.3: The SI unit of time is the second. The kelvin measures a different quantity.

questions.q: Accuracy refers to how close a reading is to
questions.explain: Accuracy is how close a reading is to the true value of the quantity being measured.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.0: Closeness to the zero mark relates to zero error, not accuracy. Accuracy is about whether a reading is correct.
notes.1: Closeness to other readings describes precision. Accuracy is about whether a reading is correct.
notes.2: The largest reading is not a standard to compare with. Accuracy is about whether a reading is correct.

questions.q: Precision refers to how close repeated readings are to
questions.explain: Precision is how close repeated readings are to one another. Precise readings may still be inaccurate.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.0: The smallest division tells how finely a scale can be read. Precision is about the spread of repeated readings.
notes.1: Closeness to the zero mark relates to zero error. Precision is about the spread of repeated readings.
notes.3: Closeness to the true value is accuracy. Precision is about the spread of repeated readings.

questions.q: The true length is 10.0 cm. Readings are 10.0, 10.1 and 9.9 cm. They are
questions.explain: The readings are all close to 10.0 cm, so they are accurate. They are also close to one another, so they are precise.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.1: All three readings are within 0.1 cm of the true value and of one another. Compare them with the true value and with each other.
notes.2: The readings differ by only 0.2 cm at most, so they are close together. Check how close they are to one another.
notes.3: Each reading is within 0.1 cm of the true value of 10.0 cm. Check how close they are to the true value.

why.right: The readings are both precise and accurate because they are close together and close to 10.0 cm.
wrong: The readings are both precise and accurate because one of them is exactly equal to 10.0 cm.
The readings are both precise and accurate because three readings were taken instead of one.

questions.q: The true mass is 50 g. Readings are 45, 45 and 46 g. They are
questions.explain: The readings 45, 45 and 46 g are close to one another, so they are precise. They are all far from 50 g, so they are not accurate.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.0: The readings agree with one another, but compare them with the true value of 50 g. They are about 5 g too low.
notes.1: These readings are far from 50 g, and they are very close to one another. Check each term again.
notes.2: The readings differ by only 1 g, so they are close together. Check how they compare with one another.

why.right: The readings are precise but not accurate because they are close together but about 5 g below 50 g.
wrong: The readings are precise but not accurate because none of them is a round number.
The readings are precise but not accurate because mass readings are less accurate than length readings.

questions.q: The true temperature is 25 °C. Readings are 12, 41 and 33 °C. They are
questions.explain: The readings 12, 41 and 33 °C are spread far apart, so they are not precise. They are also far from 25 °C, so they are not accurate.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.1: The readings range from 12 °C to 41 °C, so they are not close together. Check how they compare with one another.
notes.2: The readings are spread far apart and none is close to 25 °C. Check each term against the data.
notes.3: Each reading is between 8 °C and 16 °C away from 25 °C. None of them is close to the true value.

why.right: The readings are neither precise nor accurate because they are far apart and far from 25 °C.
wrong: The readings are neither precise nor accurate because temperature cannot be measured exactly.
The readings are neither precise nor accurate because only three readings were taken.

questions.q: Readings are close to one another but far from the true value. They are
questions.explain: Readings that are close to one another are precise. Readings that are far from the true value are not accurate.
questions.lo: Judge the accuracy and precision of a set of readings

notes.0: This swaps the two terms. Closeness to one another and closeness to the true value are described by different words.
notes.2: The readings are close to one another, so one of the two qualities is present. Check which term describes that.
notes.3: The readings are far from the true value, so they cannot have both qualities. Check which one is missing.

why.right: Readings close to each other are precise, and readings far from the true value are not accurate.
wrong: Readings close to each other are accurate, and readings far from the true value are not precise.
Readings close to each other are precise, and accuracy depends only on which instrument is used.

questions.q: Zero error is when an instrument
choices: is read from the wrong angle
reads non-zero when it should read zero
questions.explain: Zero error is when an instrument shows a reading that is not zero when it should read zero, such as an empty balance showing 2 g.
questions.lo: Identify zero error and correct readings for it

notes.0: Reading from the wrong angle causes parallax error. Zero error comes from the instrument itself before anything is measured.
notes.1: Readings that are far apart are not precise. Zero error is about what the instrument shows when nothing is being measured.
notes.3: Not being able to measure small values relates to the smallest division on the scale. Zero error is about the starting reading.

questions.q: Which function on an electronic balance removes zero error?
questions.explain: The tare function sets the display of an electronic balance back to zero. This removes zero error before the mass is measured.
questions.lo: Identify zero error and correct readings for it

notes.0: The hold function keeps a reading on the display. It does not reset the balance to zero.
notes.1: The unit function changes the unit shown, such as from g to kg. It does not reset the balance to zero.
notes.2: Switching off does not correct the starting reading. The function needed sets the display back to zero.

questions.q: A balance reads 2 g when empty. A rock reads 50 g. What is the mass of the rock?
questions.explain: The balance reads 2 g too high. The zero error is subtracted from the reading, so 50 g minus 2 g gives 48 g.
questions.lo: Identify zero error and correct readings for it

notes.1: 50 g is the reading shown, which includes the zero error. The 2 g shown when empty must be taken into account.
notes.2: Adding the zero error moves the answer further from the true mass. The balance already reads too high.
notes.3: 2 g is the zero error, not the mass of the rock. Use it to correct the rock's reading.

why.right: The rock's mass is found by subtracting the 2 g zero error from the 50 g reading.
wrong: The rock's mass is found by adding the 2 g zero error to the 50 g reading.
The rock's mass is found by ignoring the zero error because 2 g is very small.

questions.q: A scale reads −200 g with nothing on it. An apple reads 0 g. What is the mass of the apple?
questions.explain: The scale reads 200 g too low, so 200 g must be added to every reading. 0 g plus 200 g gives 200 g.
questions.lo: Identify zero error and correct readings for it

notes.0: This counts the zero error twice. The scale reads 200 g too low, so the correction only needs to be made once.
notes.2: 0 g is the reading shown, but the scale starts 200 g below zero. The reading must be corrected.
notes.3: −200 g is the zero error, not the mass of the apple. A mass cannot be negative.

why.right: The apple's mass is found by adding 200 g, since the scale reads 200 g too low.
wrong: The apple's mass is found by subtracting 200 g, since the scale shows a negative number.
The apple's mass is found by doubling 200 g, since the error affects both readings.

questions.q: A balance has a zero error of +5 g. A 30 g object is placed on it. What is the reading?
questions.explain: A zero error of +5 g means the balance reads 5 g too high. The reading is 30 g plus 5 g, which is 35 g.
questions.lo: Identify zero error and correct readings for it

notes.0: Subtracting is how a reading is corrected. This question asks what the balance shows, which includes the extra 5 g.
notes.1: 30 g is the true mass. The balance adds its zero error to every reading it shows.
notes.3: 5 g is only the zero error. The balance also measures the 30 g object.

why.right: The balance shows 35 g because a +5 g zero error adds 5 g to every reading.
wrong: The balance shows 35 g because heavier objects make the zero error grow larger.
The balance shows 35 g because the object gains 5 g of mass on the balance.

questions.q: Parallax error is caused by
choices: viewing the scale from the wrong position
questions.explain: Parallax error happens when a scale is read with the eye in the wrong position, at an angle instead of directly in line with the marking.
questions.lo: State how to avoid parallax error for common instruments

notes.0: Slow reaction time affects timing with a stopwatch. Parallax error happens while a scale is being read.
notes.1: An instrument not reading zero has zero error. Parallax error comes from the person reading the scale, not the instrument.
notes.2: Wind is a condition of the experiment that can cause unpredictable error. Parallax error happens while a scale is being read.

why.right: Parallax error happens because the reading appears to change when the scale is viewed at an angle.
wrong: Parallax error happens because the scale markings shift on the instrument when it is moved.
Parallax error happens because the instrument was not set to zero before it was used.

questions.q: When reading a measuring cylinder of water, the eye should be level with the
questions.explain: Water forms a curved surface called a meniscus that dips in the middle. The reading is taken with the eye level with the bottom of the meniscus.
questions.lo: State how to avoid parallax error for common instruments

notes.0: Water curves down in the middle, and its edges climb up the glass. Reading where the edges are gives a value that is too high.
notes.1: The eye must be level with the liquid surface being read, not the base. Looking from the base causes parallax error.
notes.3: The eye must be level with the liquid surface being read. The top of the cylinder is not where the water is.

why.right: The bottom of the meniscus is read because the water surface curves down and its lowest point gives the level.
wrong: The bottom of the meniscus is read because the top of the meniscus is too hard to see clearly.
The bottom of the meniscus is read because lower readings are always more accurate than higher ones.

questions.q: When reading a ruler, the line of sight should be
choices: at an angle from the right
at an angle from the left
questions.explain: The line of sight should be perpendicular to the ruler at the marking being read. Viewing at an angle causes parallax error.
questions.lo: State how to avoid parallax error for common instruments

notes.1: Viewing at an angle from the right makes the marking seem to shift. This gives parallax error.
notes.2: Viewing at an angle from the left makes the marking seem to shift. This gives parallax error.
notes.3: Looking along the ruler, parallel to it, makes the markings impossible to read. The eye should be directly above the mark.

why.right: Viewing a ruler perpendicular to the marking avoids parallax error because the mark does not appear to shift.
wrong: Viewing a ruler perpendicular to the marking avoids parallax error because it makes the markings look larger.
Viewing a ruler perpendicular to the marking avoids parallax error because it removes any zero error.

questions.q: A student reads a measuring cylinder while looking down from above. The reading will
questions.explain: Looking down from above means the eye is not level with the meniscus. This causes parallax error, so the reading will be wrong.
questions.lo: State how to avoid parallax error for common instruments

notes.0: Viewing from above does not make a reading more precise. It moves the eye away from the correct position.
notes.2: Zero error comes from the instrument itself. The problem here is the position of the eye.
notes.3: The eye is not level with the meniscus, so the reading will not be correct.

why.right: Reading a cylinder from above gives an error because the eye is not level with the meniscus.
wrong: Reading a cylinder from above gives an error because the scale does not start at zero.
Reading a cylinder from above gives an error because the water moves when the student leans over.

questions.q: A balance always shows 3 g more than the true mass. What type of error is this?
questions.explain: The balance shows 3 g too much every time. An error that is the same size and in the same direction each time is a consistent error.
questions.lo: Classify errors as consistent or unpredictable

notes.1: The readings differ from the true mass by 3 g, so there is an error. Look at whether it is the same every time.
notes.2: Unpredictable errors change from reading to reading. Here the error is always 3 g too high.

why.right: The balance has a consistent error because every reading is too high by the same 3 g.
wrong: The balance has a consistent error because 3 g is too small to be an unpredictable error.
The balance has a consistent error because the student takes each reading carefully.

questions.q: A student starts a stopwatch late because of reaction time. What type of error is this?
questions.explain: Reaction time is not the same each time, so the stopwatch starts late by different amounts. This makes the error unpredictable.
questions.lo: Classify errors as consistent or unpredictable

notes.0: A consistent error is the same every time. Reaction time varies from one try to the next.
notes.1: Starting the stopwatch late changes the time recorded, so there is an error.

why.right: Reaction time causes an unpredictable error because the delay is different each time the stopwatch is started.
wrong: Reaction time causes an unpredictable error because the stopwatch has a zero error that changes the reading.
Reaction time causes an unpredictable error because the student's delay is exactly the same in every trial.

questions.q: Wind makes water in one beaker evaporate faster. What type of error is this?
questions.explain: Wind does not affect every beaker in the same way or by the same amount. An error that varies like this is an unpredictable error.
questions.lo: Classify errors as consistent or unpredictable

notes.0: A consistent error affects every reading in the same way. Wind affects only one beaker, and not by a set amount.
notes.2: The faster evaporation changes the results for that beaker, so there is an error.

why.right: Wind causes an unpredictable error because it changes the results by different amounts at different times.
wrong: Wind causes an unpredictable error because evaporation can only happen when the air is moving.
Wind causes an unpredictable error because it makes every reading too high by the same amount.

questions.q: Zero error in an instrument causes readings that are
choices: sometimes too high and sometimes too low
questions.explain: Zero error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction. The readings are therefore consistently inaccurate.
questions.lo: Classify errors as consistent or unpredictable

notes.0: Readings with zero error are all shifted away from the true value. Check whether shifted readings can be accurate.
notes.1: The readings are consistent, but they are shifted away from the true value. Check whether shifted readings can be accurate.
notes.2: Readings that are sometimes too high and sometimes too low come from unpredictable errors. Zero error shifts readings the same way each time.

why.right: Zero error makes readings inaccurate because every reading is shifted from the true value by the same amount.
wrong: Zero error makes readings inaccurate because every reading is shifted by a different random amount.
Zero error makes readings inaccurate because the instrument cannot show numbers below zero.

questions.q: A student records her results as obtained, even though they do not support her hypothesis. This shows
questions.explain: Recording results honestly, even when they do not support the hypothesis, shows integrity.
questions.lo: Identify scientific attitudes from a described action

notes.0: Perseverance means continuing when a task is difficult. This student is being honest about her results.
notes.2: Creativity means coming up with new ideas. This action is about reporting results truthfully.
notes.3: Curiosity means wanting to find out more. This action is about reporting results truthfully.

why.right: Recording unexpected results as obtained shows integrity because it reports the evidence honestly.
wrong: Recording unexpected results as obtained shows integrity because it proves the hypothesis was correct.
Recording unexpected results as obtained shows integrity because it makes the experiment finish faster.

questions.q: A student repeats a difficult experiment many times until it works. This shows
questions.explain: Repeating a difficult experiment many times without giving up shows perseverance.
questions.lo: Identify scientific attitudes from a described action

notes.1: Integrity means being honest about results. This student is showing that they keep trying.
notes.2: Creativity means thinking of new ideas or methods. This student repeats the same experiment.
notes.3: Objectivity means judging evidence fairly without bias. This student is showing that they do not give up.

why.right: Repeating a hard experiment until it works shows perseverance because the student keeps trying despite difficulty.
wrong: Repeating a hard experiment until it works shows perseverance because the student changes results until they look right.
Repeating a hard experiment until it works shows perseverance because the student follows the steps without thinking.

questions.q: A student considers a classmate's different explanation before deciding. This shows
questions.explain: Considering another person's different explanation before deciding shows open-mindedness.
questions.lo: Identify scientific attitudes from a described action

notes.0: Integrity means being honest about results. This student is willing to consider a different idea.
notes.1: Perseverance means not giving up on a difficult task. This student is willing to consider a different idea.
notes.3: Creativity means coming up with new ideas. Here the student is considering someone else's idea.

why.right: Considering a classmate's explanation shows open-mindedness because other ideas are weighed before judging.
wrong: Considering a classmate's explanation shows open-mindedness because the classmate's idea must be correct.
Considering a classmate's explanation shows open-mindedness because the student has no ideas of their own.

questions.q: Where should broken glassware be discarded?
questions.explain: Broken glass is sharp and can cut people. It goes in a puncture-proof sharps container so no one is hurt when the waste is handled.
questions.lo: Apply laboratory safety rules

notes.0: Glass in the sink can cut someone and block the drain. Sharp waste needs a container it cannot cut through.
notes.1: Sharp glass can cut through a paper bag and injure someone. It needs a container it cannot pierce.
notes.2: Cleaners may not know there is glass in a normal dustbin and could be cut. Sharp waste needs a special container.

why.right: Broken glass goes in a sharps container because the container cannot be pierced, so nobody gets cut.
wrong: Broken glass goes in a sharps container because glass reacts with other waste in a normal bin.
Broken glass goes in a sharps container because glass is a toxic substance.

questions.q: A student spills a chemical on the bench. What should she do first?
choices: report it to the teacher immediately
wipe it up with her hands
questions.explain: A spill should be reported to the teacher immediately. The teacher knows how to clean up the chemical safely.
questions.lo: Apply laboratory safety rules

notes.0: Carrying on leaves the spill where others may touch it. A spill must be dealt with before the experiment continues.
notes.2: Leaving does not make the spill safe, and others may be harmed. Someone who can deal with it must be told.
notes.3: Many chemicals can burn or harm the skin. Spills should never be touched with bare hands.

why.right: A chemical spill is reported at once because the teacher knows how to clean up that chemical safely.
wrong: A chemical spill is reported at once because the student will lose marks if it is found later.
A chemical spill is reported at once because all spilled chemicals catch fire within a few minutes.

questions.q: When heating a test tube, its mouth should point
questions.explain: The contents of a heated test tube can spurt out suddenly. Pointing the mouth away from everyone keeps people safe.
questions.lo: Apply laboratory safety rules

notes.0: Hot contents can spurt out of a heated test tube. Pointing it at a classmate puts them in danger.
notes.1: Hot contents can spurt out of a heated test tube. Pointing it at your own face puts you in danger.
notes.2: Pointing the mouth down at the flame can make the contents pour out. The direction must keep spurting liquid from reaching anyone.

why.right: A heated test tube is pointed away from people because hot contents can spurt out suddenly.
wrong: A heated test tube is pointed away from people because the glass may glow too brightly to look at.
A heated test tube is pointed away from people because the flame only heats the tube from one side.

questions.q: Which is unsafe when using electrical devices?
choices: touching a plug with wet hands
questions.explain: Water conducts electricity. Touching a plug with wet hands can give an electric shock, so it is unsafe.
questions.lo: Apply laboratory safety rules

notes.0: Switching off before unplugging is a safe habit. The question asks which action is unsafe.
notes.1: Keeping devices away from water prevents electric shocks, so this is safe. The question asks for the unsafe action.
notes.3: Reporting a frayed wire is the safe thing to do. The question asks for the unsafe action.

why.right: Touching a plug with wet hands is unsafe because water can conduct electricity into the body.
wrong: Touching a plug with wet hands is unsafe because water makes the plug rust and break at once.
Touching a plug with wet hands is unsafe because wet hands make the device use more electricity.

questions.q: Why are some chemicals diluted for use in the laboratory?
choices: to make them safer to use
questions.explain: Diluted chemicals are less concentrated, so they do less harm if spilled or splashed. Dilution makes them safer to use.
questions.lo: Apply laboratory safety rules

notes.1: Diluting a chemical usually makes it react more slowly, not faster. Think about why a weaker solution is chosen in school.
notes.2: Diluting is not done to change colour. Think about what a weaker solution does to the risk of harm.
notes.3: Dilution is not done to make a chemical last longer. It lowers the concentration, so think about what that does to the risk of harm.

why.right: Diluted chemicals are used because a lower concentration does less harm if it is spilled or splashed.
wrong: Diluted chemicals are used because adding water removes the chemical completely.
Diluted chemicals are used because a lower concentration always reacts faster.

questions.q: A label warns that a substance can severely damage eyes and skin. Which hazard is this?
questions.explain: A corrosive substance can severely damage skin and eyes on contact.
questions.lo: Match a hazard symbol to the danger it warns of

notes.0: Flammable substances catch fire easily. This label warns about damage to skin and eyes.
notes.2: Explosive substances can blow up suddenly. This label warns about damage to skin and eyes.
notes.3: Oxidising substances release oxygen and can make fires worse. This label warns about damage to skin and eyes.

questions.q: A substance releases oxygen easily, which can cause fire. Which hazard is this?
questions.explain: An oxidising substance releases oxygen easily. The oxygen helps other materials burn, so it can cause or worsen a fire.
questions.lo: Match a hazard symbol to the danger it warns of

notes.1: Gas under pressure warns that a container may burst. This substance is a hazard because of what it releases.
notes.2: Corrosive substances damage skin and eyes. This substance is a hazard because it gives off a gas that helps burning.
notes.3: Environmental toxicity warns of harm to living things in nature. This substance is a hazard because of the gas it releases.

questions.q: A substance can be fatal if swallowed or breathed in. Which hazard is this?
questions.explain: Acute toxicity means a substance can cause serious harm or death quickly if it is swallowed, breathed in or touched.
questions.lo: Match a hazard symbol to the danger it warns of

notes.0: Gas under pressure warns that a container may burst or explode. This substance harms the body when taken in.
notes.1: Flammable substances catch fire easily. This substance harms the body when swallowed or breathed in.
notes.2: Oxidising substances release oxygen that helps fires. This substance harms the body when taken in.

questions.q: A substance can cause cancer or damage to organs. Which hazard is this?
questions.explain: Carcinogenicity means a substance can cause cancer. This hazard also warns of long-term damage to organs.
questions.lo: Match a hazard symbol to the danger it warns of

notes.0: Explosive substances can blow up suddenly. This substance causes long-term harm inside the body.
notes.1: Corrosive substances damage skin and eyes on contact. This substance causes long-term harm inside the body.
notes.3: Flammable substances catch fire easily. This substance causes long-term harm inside the body.

questions.q: What does the flammable hazard symbol warn of?
questions.explain: The flammable symbol warns that a substance catches fire easily. It must be kept away from flames and heat.
questions.lo: Match a hazard symbol to the danger it warns of

notes.0: Harm to the environment is shown by the environmental toxicity symbol. Think about what the word flammable means.
notes.1: Damage to skin is shown by the corrosive symbol. Think about what the word flammable means.
notes.2: Releasing oxygen is shown by the oxidising symbol. Think about what the word flammable means.

questions.q: Which is a harmful effect of plastics?
questions.explain: Most plastics do not break down easily. They build up on land and in water, causing pollution that harms living things.
questions.lo: Classify considerations as ethical, social, environmental or economic

notes.1: Being lightweight is a useful property of plastics. The question asks for a harmful effect.
notes.2: Cheap containers are a benefit of plastics. The question asks for a harmful effect.
notes.3: Being waterproof is a useful property of plastics. The question asks for a harmful effect.

why.right: Plastics cause pollution because most of them do not break down and they build up in the environment.
wrong: Plastics cause pollution because they dissolve in water and turn it into a poison.
Plastics cause pollution because they break down within days into harmful gases.

questions.q: "How much does it cost to make plastic-free utensils?" Which consideration is this?
questions.explain: Cost is about money. A question about how much something costs to make is an economic consideration.
questions.lo: Classify considerations as ethical, social, environmental or economic

notes.0: Social considerations are about how people live and use things. This question is about money.
notes.1: Ethical considerations are about what is right or wrong. This question is about money.
notes.3: Environmental considerations are about effects on nature and living things. This question is about money.

why.right: The cost question is an economic consideration because it is about the money spent to make a product.
wrong: The cost question is an economic consideration because it is about whether making the product is right.
The cost question is an economic consideration because it is about how the product affects living things.

questions.q: "How does producing plastics affect living things?" Which consideration is this?
questions.explain: Effects on living things and their surroundings are environmental considerations.
questions.lo: Classify considerations as ethical, social, environmental or economic

notes.0: Economic considerations are about money and cost. This question is about effects on living things.
notes.2: Social considerations are about how people live and use things. This question is about effects on living things in nature.
notes.3: Ethical considerations are about what is right or wrong. This question asks about effects on living things.

why.right: The question on plastics and living things is environmental because it is about effects on nature.
wrong: The question on plastics and living things is environmental because it is about the cost of plastics.
The question on plastics and living things is environmental because it is about whether people like plastics.

questions.q: "How often are plastic products used in daily life?" Which consideration is this?
questions.explain: How often people use plastic products in daily life is about people's habits and way of life. This makes it a social consideration.
questions.lo: Classify considerations as ethical, social, environmental or economic

notes.0: Environmental considerations are about effects on nature. This question is about how people live.
notes.1: Ethical considerations are about what is right or wrong. This question is about people's daily habits.
notes.3: Economic considerations are about money and cost. This question is about people's daily habits.

why.right: The question on daily plastic use is social because it is about people's habits and way of life.
wrong: The question on daily plastic use is social because it is about the money people spend.
The question on daily plastic use is social because it is about pollution of land and water.

questions.q: Which statement about science is correct?
choices: it is only done by scientists
it cannot solve every problem in the world
questions.explain: Science has limits. It cannot answer every question, such as questions of opinion, and it cannot solve every problem in the world.
questions.lo: Classify considerations as ethical, social, environmental or economic

notes.0: Questions of opinion or belief cannot be tested by experiments, so science cannot answer them.
notes.1: Anyone who observes, questions and tests ideas carefully is doing science, including students.
notes.2: Science can also be misused or have harmful side effects, such as pollution from new products.

why.right: Science cannot solve every problem because some questions involve opinions or values that cannot be tested.
wrong: Science cannot solve every problem because scientists have already stopped making new discoveries.
Science cannot solve every problem because experiments are only allowed inside a laboratory.

questions.q: Ice melts in 90 s, 60 s and 30 s in water at 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: the higher the temperature, the shorter the time
the higher the temperature, the longer the time
questions.explain: As the temperature rises from 20 °C to 60 °C, the melting time falls from 90 s to 30 s. So the higher the temperature, the shorter the time.
questions.lo: Draw conclusions from data and improve how it is presented

notes.0: No data was taken below 20 °C, so nothing can be concluded about it. A conclusion must come from the data collected.
notes.2: The melting time changes as the temperature changes, so temperature does have an effect.
notes.3: Look at the data again. As the temperature increases, check whether the time goes up or down.

why.right: The ice conclusion fits because each rise in water temperature in the data comes with a fall in melting time.
wrong: The ice conclusion fits because ice always melts faster in a larger volume of water.
The ice conclusion fits because the melting time goes up as the water temperature goes up.

questions.q: Which is the best way to show a trend in a set of readings?
questions.explain: A line graph shows how one variable changes with another. The pattern of the plotted points makes the trend easy to see.
questions.lo: Draw conclusions from data and improve how it is presented

notes.1: A drawing of the apparatus shows how the experiment was set up. It does not show the readings.
notes.2: A photograph shows what the set-up looked like, not how the readings change.
notes.3: A paragraph can list readings, but a pattern is hard to spot in text.

why.right: A line graph shows a trend best because the rise or fall of the plotted points can be seen at once.
wrong: A line graph shows a trend best because it uses more colours than a table of readings.
A line graph shows a trend best because it removes any readings that do not fit the pattern.

questions.q: Three readings were taken for each temperature. How close they are shows the
questions.explain: How close repeated readings are to one another shows their precision.
questions.lo: Draw conclusions from data and improve how it is presented

notes.0: Zero error is found by checking the instrument before measuring. It is not shown by comparing repeated readings.
notes.2: The variable changed is the temperature chosen by the student. Repeated readings do not show what was changed.
notes.3: Accuracy compares readings with the true value. Here the readings are only being compared with each other.

why.right: Close repeated readings show precision because precision is about how well readings agree with each other.
wrong: Close repeated readings show precision because close readings must also be equal to the true value.
Close repeated readings show precision because precision is about how small the units of the readings are.

questions.q: An investigation gives no clear conclusion. What should the student do?
questions.explain: If the results give no clear conclusion, the student should modify the investigation, for example by changing the method or taking more readings, and test again.
questions.lo: Draw conclusions from data and improve how it is presented

notes.1: Removing readings that disagree hides real evidence. Every result must be recorded honestly.
notes.2: Making up data is dishonest and breaks scientific integrity. Conclusions must come from real results.
notes.3: Copying results is dishonest. The student needs real evidence from their own investigation.

why.right: Modifying the investigation helps because a better method can give reliable evidence for a clear conclusion.
wrong: Modifying the investigation helps because it lets the student change the results to match the hypothesis.
Modifying the investigation helps because an unclear result means the hypothesis was certainly true.
